title: Journalism
description: Free Journalism study guide: 8 units, 320 practice questions, 80 flashcards, quick reference, memory tricks, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

units.name: What Makes News

concepts.intro: Editors decide what becomes news by weighing a shared set of news values against each other; a story rarely needs all of them, but the strongest stories carry several at once.
b: Timeliness: recent events beat old ones — 'news' literally means new
Proximity: events closer to the audience (geographically or culturally) feel more relevant
Impact/consequence: how many people are affected and how seriously
Prominence: well-known people or institutions make ordinary events newsworthy
Conflict: disagreement, competition, or controversy draws attention
Human interest: emotionally engaging stories about ordinary people

concepts.intro: Unusual or unexpected events are newsworthy precisely because they break from routine — 'dog bites man' is not news, but 'man bites dog' is.
b: Novelty covers firsts, records, and rare occurrences
Oddity relies on violating audience expectations
Overused novelty angles can trivialize serious topics
Editors must balance oddity against genuine significance
Novelty alone rarely justifies front-page placement without other values

concepts.intro: The news cycle is the ongoing process by which stories are reported, updated, and eventually replaced by newer developments.
b: 24-hour digital cycles have replaced the old once-daily print cycle
Breaking news gets updated continuously as facts emerge
Follow-up stories add context, reaction, and consequence over days
Social media can compress the cycle to minutes
Speed pressure increases the risk of reporting errors

concepts.intro: Hard news covers timely, significant events (crime, politics, disasters); soft news covers lifestyle, entertainment, and human-interest topics with less time pressure.
b: Hard news is typically written in inverted-pyramid style
Soft news allows more narrative and creative structure
Hard news usually runs quickly; soft news can run anytime
Both require the same standards of accuracy and sourcing
The line between them blurs in feature-style hard-news coverage

concepts.intro: Editors act as gatekeepers, deciding which stories reach the public; by choosing what to cover, the press also shapes what audiences think about (agenda-setting), even if not what to think.
b: Gatekeeping happens at every stage: pitch, assignment, edit, and publish
Agenda-setting theory holds that media prominence signals importance to the public
Social media has distributed gatekeeping beyond traditional editors
News judgment reflects a newsroom's values and audience
Bias can enter through story selection, not just wording

keyFacts: The core news values are timeliness, proximity, impact, prominence, conflict, novelty, and human interest.
A story's newsworthiness usually comes from combining several values, not just one.
Gatekeeping is the editorial process of deciding which stories get published.
Agenda-setting theory says media coverage influences what topics the public considers important.
traps: Confusing 'interesting to me' with 'newsworthy' — newsworthiness depends on audience relevance, not personal curiosity
Treating oddity as sufficient on its own; unusual is not automatically important
Assuming proximity only means physical distance — cultural and community proximity count too
Forgetting that agenda-setting theory is about influencing what people think about, not what they think

units.name: News Writing & Inverted Pyramid

concepts.intro: The inverted pyramid structures a news story from most to least important information, so editors can cut from the bottom and readers get the key facts immediately.
b: Most newsworthy facts appear first, least important last
Allows editors to trim length from the bottom without losing essentials
Suits skimming readers who may not finish the article
Contrasts with chronological or narrative storytelling structures
Originated partly from unreliable telegraph transmission during the Civil War era

concepts.intro: The lead is the opening sentence or paragraph that summarizes the story's most essential information and hooks the reader.
b: A summary lead answers the most important of the Five Ws and H
Hard-news leads are typically one sentence, 25-35 words
Feature leads (delayed/anecdotal) can defer the main point for effect
A strong lead avoids burying the news under minor details
Leads should avoid starting with a quote or a question in hard news

concepts.intro: Who, What, When, Where, Why, and How are the essential questions every basic news story must answer.
b: Who: the people or organizations involved
What: the event or action that occurred
When and Where: the time and location
Why: the cause or motivation behind the event
How: the manner in which it happened
Not every W needs to be in the lead — prioritize the most newsworthy ones

concepts.intro: The nut graf (nutshell paragraph) follows the lead to explain why the story matters, then the body elaborates with supporting facts and quotes in descending importance.
b: Nut graf gives context and significance the lead couldn't fit
Body paragraphs should each carry one clear idea
Supporting quotes should reinforce, not just repeat, the facts
Background/context info sits lower since it's less time-sensitive
Transitions guide the reader logically between related facts

concepts.l: AP Style and News Writing Mechanics
concepts.intro: AP Style is the standard style guide most U.S. newsrooms use for consistency in grammar, punctuation, abbreviations, and numerals.
b: Numbers one through nine are spelled out; 10 and above use numerals
Titles are capitalized before a name, lowercase after
Attribution typically uses 'said,' not more dramatic synonyms
Avoid editorializing adjectives; let facts speak for themselves
Consistent style builds credibility and reader trust

concepts.intro: Every factual claim in a news story should be attributed to a clear, identifiable source so readers can judge its credibility.
b: Direct quotes must be word-for-word accurate
Paraphrased information still needs attribution
Attribution should come early in a sentence when the source matters
Avoid anonymous sourcing unless justified and approved by editors
Never present opinion as unattributed fact in a news story

keyFacts: The inverted pyramid places the most newsworthy information first, least important last.
A hard-news lead should answer the most important of the Five Ws and H in one concise sentence.
The nut graf explains why a story matters, right after the lead.
AP Style provides the standardized grammar, punctuation, and formatting rules most U.S. newsrooms follow.
traps: Burying the lead — putting the most important fact several paragraphs in, not right at the top
Writing a lead that tries to answer all six Ws at once instead of prioritizing the most newsworthy ones
Using dramatic attribution verbs like 'claimed' or 'admitted' instead of the neutral 'said'
Treating the nut graf as optional filler rather than the paragraph that justifies the story's importance

units.name: Interviewing Skills

concepts.intro: Strong interviews start before the recorder turns on: research the subject, define your goal, and draft flexible questions.
b: Research the subject's background, prior statements, and public record
Identify the story's central question the interview must answer
Draft open-ended questions but stay ready to improvise
Decide on setting, timing, and recording method in advance
Anticipate sensitive topics and plan how to raise them respectfully

concepts.intro: Open-ended questions invite detailed, reflective answers, while closed questions elicit short factual confirmations — skilled interviewers use both strategically.
b: Open questions ('How did that feel?') encourage elaboration and quotes
Closed questions ('Did you sign the contract?') confirm specific facts
Leading questions that suggest an answer should be avoided
Follow-up questions probe deeper into unclear or evasive answers
Silence after a question can prompt a source to keep talking

concepts.intro: Effective interviewers listen more than they talk, catching details that spark better follow-up questions than any pre-written list.
b: Maintain eye contact and minimal interruptions to build rapport
Note surprising or vague statements for immediate follow-up
Avoid rigidly following a script when a better angle emerges
Paraphrasing an answer back can confirm understanding and get clarity
Take detailed notes even when recording, in case of technical failure

concepts.intro: Evasive, hostile, or emotionally distressed sources require patience, tact, and persistence without crossing ethical lines.
b: Rephrase a dodged question rather than abandoning it
Stay calm and professional even if a source becomes defensive
Give grieving or traumatized sources space and let them decline questions
Avoid badgering; repeated respectful follow-ups work better than pressure
Know when to end an interview that has become unproductive or unsafe

concepts.l: On/Off the Record and Attribution Levels
concepts.intro: Sources and reporters must agree clearly on ground rules before information is shared, since these terms govern how it can be used.
b: On the record: everything can be quoted and attributed by name
On background: information can be used but not attributed to the named source
On deep background: information can be used but with no attribution at all
Off the record: information cannot be published at all
Ground rules must be agreed upon before the information is shared, not after

keyFacts: Effective interviews rely on preparation: research the subject and identify the story's key question beforehand.
Open-ended questions draw out detail and reflection; closed questions confirm specific facts.
The four attribution levels are on the record, on background, on deep background, and off the record.
Ground rules for attribution must be negotiated before information is shared, not retroactively.
traps: Asking leading questions that suggest the desired answer instead of neutral open questions
Assuming 'off the record' means the same as 'not for attribution' — they are different levels
Sticking rigidly to a prepared question list instead of following up on unexpected answers
Agreeing to off-the-record terms after the source has already revealed the information

units.name: Fact-Checking & Ethics

concepts.intro: The Society of Professional Journalists' Code of Ethics organizes journalistic responsibility into four core principles that guide everyday newsroom decisions.
b: Seek truth and report it: verify information and provide context
Minimize harm: treat sources, subjects, and the vulnerable with compassion
Act independently: avoid conflicts of interest and outside influence
Be accountable and transparent: acknowledge errors and explain decisions
The code is a set of aspirational guidelines, not enforceable law

concepts.intro: Before publishing, journalists must independently confirm claims using multiple, credible, ideally primary sources.
b: Cross-check facts with at least two independent sources when possible
Prefer primary sources (documents, direct witnesses) over secondary ones
Verify names, titles, dates, numbers, and quotes exactly
Be skeptical of viral or unverified social media claims
Document sourcing so claims can be defended if challenged

concepts.intro: A conflict of interest arises when a journalist's personal relationships, financial ties, or biases could compromise — or appear to compromise — their objectivity.
b: Financial ties to a story's subject must be disclosed or avoided
Personal relationships with sources can create real or perceived bias
Journalists generally avoid political activism related to their beat
Gifts or favors from sources should be declined
Even the appearance of a conflict can damage credibility

concepts.intro: Plagiarism (using others' work without credit) and fabrication (inventing facts, quotes, or sources) are among journalism's most serious ethical violations.
b: Plagiarism includes copying text, ideas, or structure without attribution
Fabrication includes invented quotes, composite characters, or fake events
Both violations can end careers and destroy outlet credibility
Proper attribution and original reporting prevent plagiarism
Corrections cannot fix fabrication — it requires retraction and accountability

concepts.intro: When errors occur, credible news organizations promptly and transparently correct the record rather than quietly editing or ignoring mistakes.
b: Corrections should be clearly labeled and explain what was wrong
Minor typos may be fixed silently; substantive errors require a formal correction
Transparency about mistakes builds long-term audience trust
Ombudsmen or public editors at some outlets review complaints independently
Failing to correct known errors is itself an ethical failure

keyFacts: The SPJ Code of Ethics rests on four pillars: seek truth and report it, minimize harm, act independently, and be accountable and transparent.
Facts should be verified with multiple independent, preferably primary, sources before publication.
A conflict of interest can damage credibility even if it's only a perceived, not actual, bias.
Fabrication (inventing facts or quotes) is a more severe violation than a simple factual error and typically ends careers.
traps: Confusing plagiarism (uncredited copying) with fabrication (inventing information) — both are serious but distinct violations
Assuming a single source is enough verification for a significant or controversial claim
Believing the SPJ Code of Ethics is legally binding — it is a professional guideline, not law
Quietly fixing a substantive factual error without publishing a formal correction

units.name: Feature Writing

concepts.intro: Unlike hard news, features are usually built as stories with a beginning, middle, and end rather than an inverted pyramid — information is released for dramatic and emotional effect, not just efficiency.
b: The 'hourglass' and narrative arc structures replace the inverted pyramid for many features
A strong lede (anecdotal, scene-setting, or descriptive) draws the reader in before the nut graf explains why the story matters
The nut graf (or 'nut paragraph') tells the reader the point of the story after the narrative hook
Scenes, chronology, and character development pace the story like fiction, even though the facts must be true
The kicker — a strong final quote, image, or detail — closes the story with resonance
Foreshadowing and callbacks to the opening scene give features a sense of unity

concepts.intro: Human-interest features find the personal, emotional dimension of a larger issue by focusing on how it affects a specific person or small group.
b: A human-interest angle uses one person's experience as a lens onto a bigger trend or issue
Profiles are a common feature form, built around a single subject's life, work, or personality
Empathy and specificity — names, details, dialogue — make readers care about the subject
Reporters must balance emotional appeal with factual accuracy; a moving story is not an excuse to embellish
Human-interest stories often run alongside hard-news coverage of the same event to add context and emotional depth

concepts.intro: Features rely on sensory, specific detail to put readers in a scene, rather than the general summary language typical of straight news writing.
b: Show, don't tell: concrete sensory details (sight, sound, smell) work better than abstract adjectives
Specific details (a person's cracked hands, a particular smell in a room) are more credible and vivid than vague ones
Description should serve the story's point, not just decorate it
Dialogue and direct quotation, reproduced accurately, bring scenes to life
Overwriting — piling on adjectives or purple prose — can undermine credibility and clarity

concepts.intro: Feature writing covers several recognizable subgenres, each with its own conventions.
b: Profile features focus on one person's life, achievements, or personality
Trend stories identify and illustrate a pattern happening across many people or places
Human-interest features center on emotionally engaging personal stories
Explanatory/backgrounder features unpack the context behind a complex ongoing story
How-to and service features give readers practical, actionable information
Seasonal or 'evergreen' features are not tied to a specific news event and can run anytime

concepts.intro: Because features rely on scene and character, they typically demand more time-intensive reporting than a daily news story.
b: Feature reporters spend extended time observing subjects to gather authentic scenes and quotes
Detailed notes on setting, appearance, and behavior support later descriptive writing
Multiple interviews, sometimes over weeks, build a fuller picture of a subject
Fact-checking remains as rigorous as hard news — narrative style never excuses inaccuracy
Feature writers still need a clear focus or theme (a 'nut graf' idea) before drafting, to avoid a meandering story

keyFacts: The inverted pyramid is replaced in features by narrative structures like the hourglass, where an anecdotal lede leads into a nut graf that states the story's significance.
A 'nut graf' explains why the story matters and what it is really about, usually placed after the opening scene or anecdote.
Human-interest stories use one person's specific experience to illuminate a broader issue or trend.
Features demand the same factual accuracy as hard news; vivid, specific detail — not invented detail — creates believability.
traps: A feature can bury the lede with a long anecdote and no nut graf, not skip factual verification — accuracy standards do not relax in feature writing.
Descriptive detail should be concrete and specific ('rust-streaked gutters'), not vague adjectives ('a nice old house').
A kicker is the story's closing line or image, not a quick summary paragraph like a hard-news story's ending.
Human interest means finding the personal angle on real events, not fabricating composite characters or invented scenes for effect.

units.name: Opinion vs News

concepts.intro: A fact is a statement that can be verified as true or false with evidence; an opinion expresses a belief, judgment, or interpretation that cannot be proven the same way.
b: Facts are verifiable through documents, data, records, or direct observation
Opinions rely on values, preferences, or interpretation and can vary between people
News reporting should stick to verifiable facts and attributed claims, not the reporter's judgments
Opinion writing is explicitly labeled as opinion, editorial, or commentary so readers know the difference
A statement can mix fact and opinion, e.g. 'the mayor raised taxes' (fact) 'which was reckless' (opinion)

concepts.intro: An editorial is an unsigned opinion piece that represents the official position of a publication, typically written or approved by an editorial board separate from the newsroom.
b: Editorials are institutional opinions, not the view of any single reporter
Most publications keep a wall of separation between the editorial board and the news reporting staff
Editorials often argue for a specific action or position, such as endorsing a candidate or policy
They typically appear on a dedicated 'opinion' or 'editorial' page, clearly separated from news
Editorial boards may include publishers, senior editors, and sometimes community members

concepts.intro: An op-ed ('opposite the editorial page') is a signed opinion piece written by someone outside the editorial board, while a column is a recurring, signed piece reflecting one writer's consistent viewpoint.
b: Op-eds are typically submitted by outside experts, politicians, or public figures, not staff editors
Columns run regularly and are tied to one writer's byline and voice
Both op-eds and columns must be clearly labeled as opinion content
Op-ed writers are still expected to support their arguments with accurate facts and evidence
News organizations often have separate editorial standards and fact-checking processes for opinion content

concepts.intro: Objectivity is the journalistic standard of reporting facts without personal bias, while balance means fairly representing relevant perspectives on a controversy.
b: Objectivity does not mean 'no viewpoint exists' — it means the reporter's own opinion should not shape the reporting
Balance requires including significant, relevant viewpoints, not necessarily equal space to every claim
False balance occurs when a fringe or unsupported view is given equal weight to a well-evidenced one
Objectivity is upheld through sourcing, attribution, and separating fact from interpretation
Some newsrooms now favor 'fairness' or 'accuracy' over strict objectivity, while still avoiding advocacy in news stories

concepts.intro: Bias can enter news coverage through word choice, story selection, source selection, and framing, even without an explicit statement of opinion.
b: Loaded language (e.g., 'regime' vs. 'government') can signal bias without stating an opinion directly
Story selection bias occurs when certain topics are consistently covered or ignored
Source selection bias happens when only one side's experts or witnesses are quoted
Framing bias shapes how an issue is presented, such as emphasizing conflict over cooperation
Critical readers check for attribution, multiple sources, and loaded language to spot bias
Confirmation bias in audiences can make biased coverage feel 'objective' if it matches existing beliefs

keyFacts: News reporting presents verifiable, attributed facts; opinion content (editorials, op-eds, columns) is explicitly labeled and argues a viewpoint.
An editorial represents a publication's institutional position, decided by an editorial board, separate from the newsroom that reports the news.
An op-ed is a signed opinion piece from someone outside the publication's staff; a column is a recurring signed piece by one writer.
Bias can appear in reporting through word choice, story selection, source selection, and framing, even when no explicit opinion is stated.
traps: An editorial reflects the publication's institutional stance, not the personal opinion of an individual reporter.
Objectivity means keeping the reporter's own opinion out of the story, not pretending that no legitimate viewpoints exist.
Balance means including significant, relevant perspectives, not giving equal weight to a fringe claim and a well-evidenced one (false balance).
Op-eds must still be factually accurate; being labeled 'opinion' permits argument and interpretation, not fabrication.

units.name: Media Law Basics

concepts.intro: Defamation is a false statement presented as fact that damages someone's reputation; libel is written/published defamation, while slander is spoken defamation.
b: To prove defamation, a plaintiff generally must show a false statement of fact, publication to a third party, identification, and damage to reputation
Truth is an absolute defense against a defamation claim in the U.S.
Public officials and public figures must prove 'actual malice' — that the publisher knew the statement was false or acted with reckless disregard for the truth (New York Times v. Sullivan, 1964)
Private individuals generally only need to prove negligence, a lower standard than actual malice
Opinion, clearly labeled as such, is generally protected and cannot be defamatory if it doesn't imply false facts
Retractions and corrections can limit damages but do not automatically erase liability

concepts.intro: Shield laws protect journalists from being legally compelled to reveal confidential sources or unpublished material in court.
b: Shield laws vary by state; there is no comprehensive federal shield law in the U.S.
They exist to protect the free flow of information by letting sources speak without fear of exposure
Protections are not absolute — courts can sometimes compel disclosure in criminal cases or when no other source can provide the information
Confidentiality promises to sources are treated as serious ethical commitments even when legal protection is limited
Reporters who refuse court orders to reveal sources can face contempt of court charges, including fines or jail time

concepts.intro: Prior restraint is government action that blocks speech or publication before it happens, rather than punishing it afterward; U.S. courts treat it as the most serious First Amendment violation.
b: The Supreme Court has held prior restraint is presumptively unconstitutional and requires an extremely high burden of justification
New York Times Co. v. United States (1971, the 'Pentagon Papers' case) rejected the government's attempt to block publication of classified material
Courts generally prefer to let material be published and pursue after-the-fact remedies (like defamation suits) rather than censor in advance
National security claims alone are not automatically sufficient to justify prior restraint
Prior restraint differs from post-publication liability, which punishes a publisher after the fact for content already published

concepts.intro: FOIA is a federal law giving the public and press the right to request access to records held by federal government agencies, with state-level equivalents for state and local records.
b: FOIA requests can be filed by anyone, not just journalists, to obtain government records
Agencies must generally respond within a set statutory timeframe, though delays are common in practice
FOIA includes specific exemptions, such as national security, personal privacy, and law enforcement investigations
State versions of FOIA (often called 'sunshine laws' or open-records laws) apply to state and local government records
FOIA is a key investigative journalism tool for uncovering government documents, data, and communications

concepts.intro: Beyond defamation, journalists must navigate privacy law and other legal limits when gathering and publishing information about individuals.
b: Invasion of privacy can include intrusion upon seclusion, public disclosure of private facts, and false light
Newsworthiness is a key defense: information of legitimate public concern is generally protected even if private
Trespassing or using hidden recording devices to gather news can create separate legal liability, distinct from what is ultimately published
Many states have laws governing consent for recording conversations (one-party vs. two-party consent states)
Copyright law limits the unauthorized reuse of others' photos, video, or text, separate from defamation or privacy concerns

keyFacts: Libel is written defamation; slander is spoken defamation. Truth is an absolute defense to both.
Public officials and public figures must prove 'actual malice' (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth) to win a defamation case, per New York Times v. Sullivan (1964).
Prior restraint — blocking publication before it happens — is presumptively unconstitutional and was rejected in the Pentagon Papers case, New York Times Co. v. United States (1971).
FOIA lets the public and press request federal government records, subject to specific exemptions; state open-records laws cover state and local records.
traps: Libel is written defamation and slander is spoken defamation, not interchangeable terms for the same thing.
Public figures must prove actual malice, not mere negligence — private individuals face the lower negligence standard, not the other way around.
Shield laws vary by state and are not absolute; there is no comprehensive federal shield law protecting all journalists in all situations.
FOIA gives a right to request records, not an unconditional right to receive them — exemptions like national security and privacy can justify withholding.

units.name: Digital Storytelling

concepts.intro: Digital journalism combines text, photography, video, audio, and interactive graphics to tell stories in the format best suited to the content, rather than relying on text alone.
b: Multimedia packages let editors choose the best medium for each part of a story (e.g., video for action, graphics for data, text for analysis)
Interactive graphics let readers explore data or scenarios themselves, such as maps or searchable databases
Live blogs provide continuously updated, chronological coverage of breaking events
Podcasts and audio journalism allow long-form, voice-driven storytelling distinct from written articles
Mobile-first design considerations (short paragraphs, vertical video, fast load times) shape how digital stories are built

concepts.intro: Search engine optimization (SEO) is the practice of structuring content so it is more easily found through search engines, helping journalism reach readers who are actively searching for information.
b: Clear, descriptive headlines that include relevant keywords help search engines and readers understand a story's topic
Metadata (title tags, meta descriptions) summarizes a page's content for search engine results pages
Structuring articles with subheadings and clear paragraphs improves readability and searchability
SEO should never override accuracy or ethics — 'clickbait' headlines that mislead readers damage credibility
Internal links to related stories keep readers on a site longer and helps search engines understand site structure
Search intent (what a searcher is actually trying to find) should guide how a story is framed and titled

concepts.intro: Social media has become both a newsgathering tool and a publishing platform, raising ethical questions about verification, transparency, and a journalist's personal versus professional voice.
b: Content found on social media (photos, videos, claims) must still be verified before republication, just like any other source
Reverse image searches and metadata checks help confirm whether social media content is authentic and correctly dated
Journalists must consider how personal opinions posted on social media can affect perceptions of their outlet's objectivity
Many newsrooms have explicit social media policies governing what staff can post, especially about topics they cover
Engaging with audiences on social media (replying, correcting errors publicly) is part of modern accountability journalism
Speed pressure on social media increases the risk of spreading unverified information or misinformation

concepts.intro: Data journalism uses data analysis and visualization to uncover and communicate stories, often paired with interactive tools that let readers investigate the data themselves.
b: Data journalists must verify the source, methodology, and limitations of any dataset before publishing conclusions from it
Visualizations (charts, maps, timelines) should accurately represent data without misleading scale or cherry-picked ranges
Interactive tools can let readers filter data relevant to their own location or interests
Open data portals and FOIA requests are common sources for original data journalism projects
Clear sourcing and methodology notes let readers evaluate a data story's reliability

concepts.intro: Digital storytelling introduces new verification challenges, from manipulated images to AI-generated content, requiring updated tools and standards.
b: Reverse image search tools help detect recycled or out-of-context photos and videos
Deepfakes and AI-generated images/video pose a growing verification challenge for newsrooms
Digital manipulation of photos (beyond basic cropping/color correction) violates most newsroom photo ethics policies
Corrections and updates should be clearly marked and timestamped on digital articles, since online content can be edited invisibly
Archiving original versions of digital content (via screenshots or web archiving tools) helps preserve evidence before it can be altered or deleted

keyFacts: Multimedia storytelling matches each part of a story to its best format — video, interactive graphics, audio, or text — rather than defaulting to text alone.
SEO means writing clear, keyword-relevant headlines and structured content so search engines and readers can find accurate journalism, without resorting to misleading clickbait.
Content sourced from social media must be independently verified (e.g., via reverse image search) before republication, exactly like any other source.
Digital corrections should be clearly marked and timestamped, since online articles can otherwise be edited invisibly after publication.
traps: SEO means optimizing accurate, clear headlines for discoverability, not writing misleading clickbait that inflates clicks at the expense of accuracy.
Content found on social media still requires verification before being republished — it is not automatically trustworthy just because it is public.
A journalist's personal social media posts can still affect perceptions of their outlet's objectivity, so 'personal opinion' is not fully separate from professional reporting.
Digital corrections must be clearly marked and dated; quietly editing a published article without disclosure undermines transparency, not just style.

quiz.q: Which news value refers to how recently an event occurred?
o: Timeliness
Prominence
Proximity
Conflict
quiz.e: Timeliness measures how recent an event is — 'news' means new information.

quiz.q: A local school board vote is more newsworthy to residents of that town than to people across the country because of which news value?
o: Proximity
Novelty
Prominence
Timeliness
quiz.e: Proximity means events closer to an audience, geographically or culturally, feel more relevant.

quiz.q: A celebrity's minor traffic accident becomes national news mainly because of which value?
o: Prominence
Oddity
Impact
Timeliness
quiz.e: Prominence makes events involving well-known people newsworthy even if the event itself is minor.

quiz.q: Which value measures how many people are affected by an event and how severely?
o: Impact
Conflict
Novelty
Proximity
quiz.e: Impact/consequence is about the scope and severity of an event's effects on the audience.

quiz.q: The phrase 'man bites dog' illustrates which news value?
o: Novelty/oddity
Proximity
Prominence
Conflict
quiz.e: It flips the expected 'dog bites man' scenario, showing how unusualness creates news.

quiz.q: Disagreement between political parties over a bill is newsworthy chiefly due to which value?
o: Conflict
Oddity
Timeliness
Human interest
quiz.e: Conflict — disagreement or competing interests — draws audience attention.

quiz.q: A feature about a homeless veteran finding housing relies most on which value?
o: Human interest
Prominence
Timeliness
Conflict
quiz.e: Human interest stories evoke emotion by focusing on individuals' experiences.

quiz.q: What is 'gatekeeping' in journalism?
o: The editorial process of deciding which stories get published
Fact-checking a story before publication
Blocking sources from talking to competitors
Editing a story for grammar only
quiz.e: Gatekeeping refers to editors and reporters controlling what information passes through to the public.

quiz.q: Agenda-setting theory claims the media primarily influences:
o: What topics the public thinks about
What opinions the public holds
How fast news spreads
Which advertisers buy space
quiz.e: Agenda-setting is about directing public attention to certain topics, not dictating opinions.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes hard news from soft news?
o: Hard news covers timely significant events; soft news covers lifestyle/human interest with less urgency
Hard news is always false; soft news is always true
Hard news is only online; soft news is only print
There is no meaningful difference
quiz.e: Hard news is urgent and consequential; soft news covers less time-sensitive lifestyle topics.

quiz.q: The 24-hour news cycle mainly changed journalism by:
o: Compressing the time between an event and its report and update
Eliminating the need for editors
Making print newspapers obsolete overnight
Removing the need for sourcing
quiz.e: Digital and broadcast media allow near-continuous updates rather than a single daily cycle.

quiz.q: Which is a risk created by speed pressure in the news cycle?
o: Increased chance of factual errors
Decreased audience interest
Guaranteed better writing
Elimination of gatekeeping
quiz.e: Racing to publish first raises the risk of unverified or incorrect information reaching the public.

quiz.q: A story about a rare total solar eclipse visible locally combines which two values most clearly?
o: Novelty and proximity
Conflict and prominence
Impact and timeliness
Human interest and oddity
quiz.e: The eclipse is rare (novelty) and visible to the local audience (proximity).

quiz.q: Which statement about news values is most accurate?
o: Strong stories often combine multiple news values rather than relying on just one
Every story must have all seven news values to be published
Timeliness is the only value editors consider
Novelty guarantees a story is important
quiz.e: Editors weigh several values together; rarely does one value alone justify coverage.

quiz.q: Why might editors reject a story that is only 'odd' with no other news value?
o: Because oddity alone doesn't establish genuine significance
Because odd stories are always false
Because oddity violates journalism ethics
Because readers dislike unusual stories
quiz.e: Oddity can trivialize coverage if it lacks broader relevance or consequence.

quiz.q: Social media has changed gatekeeping by:
o: Distributing the power to decide what's newsworthy beyond traditional editors
Making editors the sole gatekeepers again
Eliminating the concept of news values
Making all news equally prominent
quiz.e: Anyone can now publish and amplify information, diffusing traditional editorial control.

quiz.q: A wildfire threatening thousands of homes is newsworthy primarily because of:
o: Impact
Novelty
Prominence
Human interest only
quiz.e: The scale of consequence to many people defines impact as a news value.

quiz.q: Which is an example of hard news?
o: A city council approves an emergency budget cut
A profile of a local baker's 40-year career
A weekend recipe roundup
A review of a new movie
quiz.e: Government action with immediate consequence is a hard-news topic requiring prompt coverage.

quiz.q: Which is an example of soft news?
o: A feature on a hobbyist beekeeper
Breaking coverage of a plane crash
A city's declaration of a state of emergency
A stock market crash report
quiz.e: Lifestyle/human-interest features are soft news, without the same time pressure as breaking events.

quiz.q: The main criticism of agenda-setting theory in the social media era is that:
o: Multiple platforms and algorithms now share agenda-setting power with traditional media
It no longer applies at all
It proves media never influences audiences
It only applies to print newspapers
quiz.e: Algorithms and user-driven platforms now also shape which topics gain attention.

quiz.q: A story is timely if it:
o: Reports on recent or ongoing events
Involves a famous person
Is emotionally engaging
Breaks audience expectations
quiz.e: Timeliness specifically concerns how recent or current the information is.

quiz.q: Which best explains why prominence matters as a news value?
o: Audiences care more about the actions of well-known people or institutions
Prominent people are always more truthful
Prominence guarantees higher impact
Prominent stories require less fact-checking
quiz.e: Fame or influence raises public interest even in otherwise ordinary events.

quiz.q: Cultural proximity means a story feels relevant to an audience because of:
o: Shared identity, language, or community ties, not just geography
Physical closeness only
The story's length
The reporter's opinion
quiz.e: Proximity includes cultural or community connection, not solely physical distance.

quiz.q: Which scenario best demonstrates conflict as a news value?
o: Two candidates clash over policy in a heated debate
A parade celebrates a town's founding
A museum opens a new exhibit
A school holds a routine fire drill
quiz.e: Conflict involves disagreement or competition between parties, drawing news interest.

quiz.q: Follow-up stories in the news cycle typically add:
o: Context, reaction, and consequence after initial breaking coverage
Entirely new unrelated topics
Only corrections of prior stories
Advertising content
quiz.e: Once the initial facts are reported, follow-ups deepen understanding of a story's effects.

quiz.q: Why is 'novelty' considered a weaker standalone news value than others like impact?
o: Because being unusual doesn't necessarily mean a story matters to many people
Because novel stories are always fabricated
Because novelty is banned by ethics codes
Because novelty stories take longer to write
quiz.e: An odd occurrence may lack the broader relevance or consequence that impact provides.

quiz.q: Editorial 'news judgment' is best defined as:
o: The internal standards a newsroom uses to decide what and how to cover stories
A legal requirement for all journalists
A single universal checklist all outlets must use
A synonym for objectivity
quiz.e: News judgment reflects a specific newsroom's values, audience, and priorities.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the traditional core news values?
o: Popularity on social media
Timeliness
Proximity
Conflict
quiz.e: Social media popularity is a modern metric, not one of the traditional core news values.

quiz.q: A story about a small town's first traffic light in 50 years primarily uses which value?
o: Novelty
Conflict
Prominence
Impact
quiz.e: This is newsworthy chiefly because it's unusual/rare for that community.

quiz.q: How does bias most often enter news coverage through gatekeeping?
o: Through the selection of which stories to cover, not just how they are worded
Only through outright lying
Only through photo captions
It cannot happen through gatekeeping
quiz.e: Choosing what to cover and what to ignore itself reflects and shapes perspective.

quiz.q: Which statement about hard news writing style is accurate?
o: It typically uses the inverted pyramid to front-load the most important facts
It always uses a narrative arc with a twist ending
It avoids attribution to sources
It is written only in first person
quiz.e: Hard news relies on the inverted pyramid to deliver key facts immediately.

quiz.q: A tornado destroying a neighborhood combines which two news values most strongly?
o: Impact and timeliness
Novelty and prominence
Conflict and human interest
Proximity and oddity only
quiz.e: The disaster affects many people severely (impact) and is breaking, current news (timeliness).

quiz.q: What best describes 'human interest' journalism?
o: Stories that emphasize personal, emotional, or relatable experiences of individuals
Stories about government budgets
Stories entirely made of statistics
Stories that must be negative
quiz.e: Human interest centers on the emotional and personal dimension of a story.

quiz.q: Why do editors sometimes downplay a highly odd but insignificant story?
o: Because newsroom space and attention are limited and should favor consequential stories
Because odd stories are illegal to publish
Because audiences never enjoy odd stories
Because oddity contradicts timeliness
quiz.e: Finite resources mean editors prioritize stories combining more meaningful news values.

quiz.q: A story that a small local business reached its 100th year matters mainly through which value combined with proximity?
o: Novelty
Conflict
Prominence
Timeliness
quiz.e: Reaching a rare milestone (novelty) resonates especially with the local community (proximity).

quiz.q: The term 'breaking news' refers to:
o: A story being reported as events are still unfolding
Any story published before noon
A story that has been fully investigated over months
An opinion column
quiz.e: Breaking news denotes real-time coverage of a developing event.

quiz.q: Which is the best definition of impact/consequence as a news value?
o: The scope and severity of how an event affects an audience
How famous the people involved are
How strange the event is
How quickly the story was published
quiz.e: Impact concerns the size and seriousness of an event's effects.

quiz.q: A newsroom's decision to run five stories about a hurricane and none about a minor court case demonstrates:
o: Gatekeeping and agenda-setting in action
A factual error
A violation of libel law
An example of soft news
quiz.e: The choice of coverage volume shapes what audiences perceive as important — agenda-setting via gatekeeping.

quiz.q: Which factor is LEAST likely to make a routine city council meeting newsworthy?
o: The meeting followed standard procedure with no controversy or new information
The council voted on a major tax increase
A council member was involved in a public scandal
The meeting resulted in a controversial policy change
quiz.e: Routine, uneventful proceedings lack the news values (conflict, impact, novelty) that create newsworthiness.

quiz.q: Which best summarizes the relationship between news values and story selection?
o: Editors combine multiple news values to judge which stories deserve coverage and prominence
News values are legal requirements enforced by regulators
Only one news value can apply to a single story
News values apply only to breaking news, not features
quiz.e: News values work together as an evaluative framework editors apply across all story types.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of the inverted pyramid structure?
o: To present information from most to least important
To build suspense toward a twist ending
To organize a story chronologically
To save space for advertisements
quiz.e: The inverted pyramid front-loads the most newsworthy facts so readers get them first.

quiz.q: Why is the inverted pyramid useful for editors?
o: It lets them cut the story from the bottom without losing essential facts
It requires no editing at all
It guarantees the story is objective
It eliminates the need for a headline
quiz.e: Because least-important details are last, trimming for space is easy.

quiz.q: What is a 'lead' (or 'lede') in a news story?
o: The opening sentence or paragraph summarizing the most essential information
The final paragraph of a story
A synonym for headline
The reporter's byline
quiz.e: The lead is the crucial opening that hooks readers with the core news.

quiz.q: A typical hard-news summary lead is usually:
o: One sentence, about 25-35 words
At least three paragraphs long
Written as a question
A direct quote from a source
quiz.e: Hard-news leads are concise, single-sentence summaries of the key facts.

quiz.q: Which of the Five Ws and H answers 'the cause or motivation'?
o: Why
What
Who
How
quiz.e: 'Why' explains the reason or cause behind an event.

quiz.q: Which of the Five Ws and H covers 'the manner in which something happened'?
o: How
When
Where
Who
quiz.e: 'How' describes the process or method of the event.

quiz.q: Must every lead include all Five Ws and H?
o: No, only the most newsworthy elements should be prioritized
Yes, always include all six
No, leads should exclude all Ws
Yes, but only in feature writing
quiz.e: Overloading a lead with every W often buries the key point; prioritize what's most newsworthy.

quiz.q: What is a 'nut graf'?
o: The paragraph, usually after the lead, that explains why the story matters
The last paragraph of a story
A quote used as a headline
A correction printed later
quiz.e: The nut graf ('nutshell paragraph') gives context and significance beyond the lead.

quiz.q: In inverted-pyramid body paragraphs, information should generally be organized by:
o: Descending order of importance
Alphabetical order of sources
Chronological order only
Random order for variety
quiz.e: Each paragraph moving down the story should carry decreasingly critical information.

quiz.q: What does AP Style mainly standardize?
o: Grammar, punctuation, abbreviations, and numeral usage in news writing
The political opinions in editorials
The specific topics a newsroom must cover
Photo composition rules
quiz.e: AP Style is the industry style guide covering writing mechanics for consistency.

quiz.q: Under AP Style, how are the numbers one through nine typically written?
o: Spelled out (one, two, three...)
Always as numerals (1, 2, 3...)
Written in Roman numerals
Omitted entirely
quiz.e: AP Style spells out one through nine and uses numerals for 10 and above.

quiz.q: Which verb is the AP Style-preferred neutral choice for attribution?
o: Said
Claimed
Admitted
Insisted
quiz.e: 'Said' is neutral and doesn't imply doubt or admission of guilt, unlike more dramatic verbs.

quiz.q: Why should reporters avoid words like 'claimed' or 'admitted' in routine attribution?
o: They can imply doubt or guilt not supported by facts
They are grammatically incorrect
They are too short
AP Style bans all attribution verbs
quiz.e: Those verbs carry connotations that can bias the reader's interpretation.

quiz.q: What must be true of a direct quotation in a news story?
o: It must be word-for-word accurate
It can be paraphrased for clarity
It never needs attribution
It should be edited for grammar without notice
quiz.e: Direct quotes require exact wording; changes should use paraphrase or brackets/ellipses per style rules.

quiz.q: Does paraphrased information still require attribution?
o: Yes, all factual claims should be attributed to a clear source
No, only direct quotes need attribution
No, attribution is optional in hard news
Only when the source is anonymous
quiz.e: Even paraphrased facts must be traceable to a source for credibility.

quiz.q: 'Burying the lead' means:
o: Placing the most important fact too far down in the story
Writing too short a headline
Quoting too many sources
Omitting a byline
quiz.e: This classic writing error hides the key news value beneath less-important details.

quiz.q: Why did the inverted pyramid partly originate from telegraph-era reporting?
o: Telegraph transmissions could be cut off, so reporters front-loaded key facts
Telegraphs required stories written in verse
Telegraph operators demanded chronological order
It had nothing to do with telegraphs
quiz.e: Reporters put the most vital facts first in case the transmission failed midway.

quiz.q: A delayed or anecdotal lead is more likely to appear in:
o: Feature writing rather than breaking hard news
Breaking news alerts
AP Style guidelines
Headlines only
quiz.e: Feature leads can build narrative tension before revealing the main point, unlike hard-news leads.

quiz.q: Which sentence best exemplifies proper attribution placement?
o: Attribution should come early in a sentence when the source's identity matters to credibility
Attribution should always be the final word of a story
Attribution belongs only in headlines
Attribution should be removed if the quote is short
quiz.e: Placing attribution early helps readers immediately gauge the source's credibility.

quiz.q: A story about a city council meeting is 800 words; the editor needs to cut it to 400 for print. Which structure makes this easiest?
o: Inverted pyramid, since less-important content is at the bottom
Chronological narrative, since it can be cut anywhere
First-person essay, since the writer decides what matters
Q&A format, since answers can't be shortened
quiz.e: Inverted pyramid stories are designed to be trimmed from the end without losing key facts.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes a nut graf from a lead?
o: The lead states the core news; the nut graf explains its broader significance
They are the same paragraph
The nut graf always comes before the lead
The nut graf is only used in opinion pieces
quiz.e: The nut graf adds context and stakes that the concise lead can't include.

quiz.q: Under AP Style, how should a title before a name be capitalized?
o: Capitalized before the name (e.g., Mayor Jane Diaz), lowercase after (Jane Diaz, mayor)
Always capitalized regardless of position
Never capitalized
Only capitalized in headlines
quiz.e: AP Style capitalizes formal titles directly preceding a name, not when it follows.

quiz.q: Editorializing adjectives (e.g., calling a policy 'disastrous') in straight news writing are:
o: Generally avoided to let facts and attributed opinions speak for themselves
Encouraged to add color
Required by AP Style
Only allowed in headlines
quiz.e: Objective hard-news writing avoids inserting the reporter's own judgment through loaded language.

quiz.q: Which lead best follows hard-news conventions?
o: 'A fire destroyed two homes on Elm Street Tuesday night, displacing six residents.'
'Have you ever wondered what it's like to lose your home?'
'"It was terrifying," said resident Maria Lopez.'
'Once upon a time, on a quiet street...'
quiz.e: This lead directly summarizes the key facts (what, where, when, impact) in one sentence.

quiz.q: Why is starting a hard-news lead with a direct quote generally discouraged?
o: Because it can bury the essential facts the reader needs first
Because AP Style forbids all quotations
Because quotes are always inaccurate
Because leads must be exactly one word
quiz.e: A quote lead delays the core facts the reader needs immediately.

quiz.q: What role do supporting quotes play in the body of an inverted-pyramid story?
o: They reinforce or add color to facts already established, not just repeat them
They replace the need for facts entirely
They must always come before the lead
They are only used in the final paragraph
quiz.e: Good quotes add perspective or emotion beyond what the narrative facts state.

quiz.q: A story leads with a minor procedural detail and doesn't mention the school closing until paragraph six. This is an example of:
o: Burying the lead
A well-structured nut graf
Proper AP Style
Effective anecdotal leads
quiz.e: The most newsworthy fact (the closing) should have been in the lead, not buried.

quiz.q: Which numeral rule is correct under AP Style?
o: 'The team scored 12 goals' uses a numeral because 12 is 10 or above
'The team scored 12 goals' should be spelled 'twelve'
All numbers are always spelled out
All numbers are always numerals
quiz.e: AP Style uses numerals for numbers 10 and above, spelling out one through nine.

quiz.q: Which best defines 'attribution' in journalism?
o: Identifying the source of a fact, quote, or claim in a story
Deciding which photo runs with a story
Choosing a story's headline
Editing for grammar
quiz.e: Attribution ties information to its source so readers can evaluate credibility.

quiz.q: Why do reporters avoid anonymous sourcing except when justified?
o: Because named sources are more credible and accountable to readers
Because AP Style bans it completely
Because anonymous sources are always lying
Because it takes longer to write
quiz.e: Attributed, named sources let readers assess reliability; anonymity should be an exception, not default.

quiz.q: In a well-structured news story, background/context information typically appears:
o: Lower in the story, since it's less time-sensitive than the lead facts
Only in the headline
Before the lead
Never, unless the story is about history
quiz.e: Since inverted pyramid orders by newsworthiness, background context sits below the most urgent facts.

quiz.q: What distinguishes a summary lead from a delayed lead?
o: A summary lead states the main news immediately; a delayed lead builds up to it
A summary lead is always longer
A delayed lead is used only for breaking news
There's no meaningful difference
quiz.e: Summary leads front-load facts; delayed leads use narrative buildup, common in features.

quiz.q: Which of these is a correctly styled AP attribution?
o: Police said the suspect fled on foot.
Police alleged the suspect fled on foot, it is claimed.
The suspect, police insisted, fled on foot!
Fled on foot, said the police, the suspect.
quiz.e: This is a clear, neutral attribution using 'said' with proper sentence structure.

quiz.q: Why is consistency in style (like AP Style) important for a newsroom?
o: It builds credibility and helps readers trust the publication's professionalism
It prevents reporters from ever making mistakes
It is legally required by the government
It only matters for print, not digital
quiz.e: Consistent style signals professionalism and reduces reader confusion.

quiz.q: Which best completes an effective nut graf?
o: It answers 'why does this story matter to the reader?'
It restates the headline word for word
It introduces a new, unrelated topic
It always contains a direct quote
quiz.e: The nut graf's job is to justify the story's relevance and stakes.

quiz.q: A reporter writes: 'The mayor's plan is clearly a bad idea.' What's the problem?
o: It states an opinion as fact instead of attributing it to a source
It uses too many numerals
It's too short for a lead
It violates AP numeral style
quiz.e: Unattributed opinion inserted into straight news breaks objectivity standards.

quiz.q: Which sentence correctly follows AP Style numeral rules?
o: 'She has 3 dogs' should be written 'She has three dogs.'
'She has three dogs' should be written 'She has 3 dogs.'
Both are equally correct under AP Style
AP Style has no numeral rules
quiz.e: Since three is below 10, AP Style requires it spelled out.

quiz.q: The main risk of an overly long, information-packed lead is:
o: It overwhelms readers and obscures the single most important fact
It automatically violates AP Style
It makes the story too short
It eliminates the need for a nut graf
quiz.e: Cramming too much into one sentence buries the primary point.

quiz.q: Which is the best reason inverted pyramid remains standard in hard news despite digital publishing?
o: Readers often skim online, so front-loaded key facts serve them best
Print papers no longer exist
It is required by law
It eliminates the need for headlines
quiz.e: Online reading habits favor quickly scannable, front-loaded information just as print once did.

quiz.q: What should a reporter do if a source's exact quote contains a grammatical error?
o: Use it as said, or paraphrase instead of silently altering the quote
Silently correct the grammar without notice
Delete the quote entirely
Add words to make it sound better
quiz.e: Direct quotes must remain accurate; altering them without indication misrepresents the source.

quiz.q: What should a reporter do before conducting an interview?
o: Research the subject's background and define the story's central question
Write the story first, then interview to confirm it
Avoid preparing questions to stay spontaneous
Only prepare closed yes/no questions
quiz.e: Preparation ensures the reporter asks informed, relevant questions.

quiz.q: Which is an example of an open-ended question?
o: 'How did you feel when you found out?'
'Did you attend the meeting?'
'Is your name John Smith?'
'Did the vote pass?'
quiz.e: Open questions invite elaboration rather than a simple yes/no.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a closed question?
o: 'Did you sign the contract on Tuesday?'
'Walk me through what happened that day.'
'What was going through your mind?'
'Why did you decide to run for office?'
quiz.e: Closed questions seek a specific, short factual answer.

quiz.q: Why should reporters avoid leading questions?
o: They suggest a desired answer and can bias the response
They take too long to ask
They are grammatically incorrect
They are banned by AP Style
quiz.e: Leading questions can distort the source's true response by implying an answer.

quiz.q: What is the value of silence after asking a question?
o: It can prompt the source to elaborate further to fill the pause
It signals the interview is over
It is considered rude and should be avoided
It has no effect on interviews
quiz.e: Sources often add more detail to fill an uncomfortable silence.

quiz.q: Why is active listening critical during an interview?
o: It helps the reporter catch details that lead to better follow-up questions
It replaces the need for any preparation
It means the reporter should not take notes
It is only useful in feature interviews
quiz.e: Careful listening reveals openings a fixed question list might miss.

quiz.q: What should a reporter do if a source gives a vague or evasive answer?
o: Rephrase the question and follow up rather than abandoning it
Immediately end the interview
Accept the vague answer without further inquiry
Publish the vague answer as-is without noting it
quiz.e: Persistence through rephrasing can surface the needed information.

quiz.q: How should a reporter handle a grieving or traumatized source?
o: With patience, giving them space and the option to decline questions
By pressing hard for emotional quotes regardless of their wishes
By avoiding them entirely and using no comment
By recording without their knowledge
quiz.e: Compassionate handling respects the source's well-being while still allowing them to share if willing.

quiz.q: What does 'on the record' mean?
o: Everything said can be quoted and attributed to the source by name
Nothing said can be published
Information can be used but without naming the source
The interview is being video recorded
quiz.e: On the record is the most transparent level: full attribution is allowed.

quiz.q: What does 'off the record' mean?
o: The information cannot be published at all
The information can be quoted but not attributed
The information can be used only in follow-up stories
It's the same as 'on background'
quiz.e: Off the record bars the reporter from publishing that information altogether.

quiz.q: What does 'on background' typically mean?
o: Information can be used but not attributed to the named source
Information cannot be used in any form
The source must be named directly
It only applies to anonymous tips
quiz.e: On background lets the info be published, often attributed to a vaguer descriptor instead of the person's name.

quiz.q: What does 'on deep background' mean?
o: Information can be used but with no attribution at all, not even a vague description
The interview must be recorded on video
The source can be quoted directly by name
It is identical to being off the record
quiz.e: Deep background permits use of the information without any attribution, even indirect.

quiz.q: When should ground rules like 'off the record' be established?
o: Before the information is shared, not after
Only after the story is published
At the reporter's sole discretion after publication
Ground rules are unnecessary in journalism
quiz.e: Agreements about attribution must be made in advance; you can't retroactively make something off the record.

quiz.q: Why might a reporter paraphrase a source's answer back to them?
o: To confirm understanding and prompt clarification
To put words in the source's mouth
To end the interview quickly
To avoid taking notes
quiz.e: Reflecting the answer back checks accuracy and can invite more detail.

quiz.q: Why should reporters take notes even when recording an interview?
o: In case of technical failure with the recording device
Because recording is never allowed
Because notes are more accurate than recordings
Because AP Style requires it
quiz.e: Backup notes protect against lost or corrupted recordings.

quiz.q: Which best describes a follow-up question?
o: A question that probes deeper into an unclear or interesting point just raised
The very first question asked in an interview
A question sent by email after the story publishes
A question the source writes for themselves
quiz.e: Follow-ups build on what the source just said, digging past their initial answer.

quiz.q: What is a key risk of rigidly following a pre-written question list?
o: Missing better story angles that emerge from unexpected answers
Running out of time too quickly
Violating AP Style
Making the source uncomfortable
quiz.e: Flexibility lets reporters pursue more valuable information as it surfaces.

quiz.q: If a source becomes defensive or hostile, the reporter should:
o: Remain calm and professional rather than escalating
Match their tone and become confrontational
Immediately publish an unflattering story about them
Threaten to expose them
quiz.e: Professional composure keeps the interview productive and ethical.

quiz.q: When is it appropriate to end an interview early?
o: When it becomes unproductive or unsafe to continue
Never, interviews must always run their full planned length
Whenever the source asks a question back
Only if the recorder malfunctions
quiz.e: Reporters should use judgment to end interviews that are no longer useful or that pose risk.

quiz.q: Why is researching a subject's prior public statements useful before an interview?
o: It helps the reporter ask informed questions and catch inconsistencies
It guarantees the source will cooperate
It replaces the need to ask any questions
It is required by libel law
quiz.e: Background research sharpens the interview and can reveal contradictions worth exploring.

quiz.q: A source says, 'This is off the record,' after already answering the question on the record. What should the reporter do?
o: Explain that the information is already on the record since it was shared without prior agreement
Immediately delete the information from their notes
Agree it is now off the record
End the interview without explanation
quiz.e: Off-the-record status must be negotiated before the information is disclosed, not retroactively.

quiz.q: Which is the best way to phrase a neutral, non-leading question?
o: 'What happened at the meeting?'
'Wasn't the meeting a disaster?'
'You must have been furious, right?'
'Don't you think the mayor is wrong?'
quiz.e: This phrasing doesn't presuppose an answer, letting the source respond freely.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of identifying a story's central question before an interview?
o: It focuses the interview on the information most essential to the story
It ensures the interview is exactly ten minutes
It eliminates the need for follow-up questions
It satisfies a legal requirement
quiz.e: A clear central question keeps the interview purposeful and efficient.

quiz.q: Which interviewing behavior best builds rapport with a source?
o: Maintaining eye contact and listening with minimal interruption
Interrupting frequently to move faster
Reading questions off a script without eye contact
Checking a phone during the conversation
quiz.e: Attentive, respectful listening helps sources feel comfortable opening up.

quiz.q: A hostile source refuses to answer a key question three times. What is the best next step?
o: Rephrase the question and try a different angle rather than repeating it verbatim
Give up on the topic entirely after the first refusal
Threaten legal action against the source
Publish a guess at the answer without attribution
quiz.e: Skilled reframing can sometimes surface an answer that direct repetition can't.

quiz.q: Why is it risky to accept an interview entirely 'off the record'?
o: The reporter may gain no usable information for the story
It guarantees better quotes
It is illegal in most states
It automatically improves source credibility
quiz.e: If everything is off the record, none of it can be published, limiting the story's value.

quiz.q: What distinguishes 'on background' from 'on the record' most clearly?
o: On background withholds the source's name from attribution; on the record allows full naming
On background means nothing can be published
On the record means the source must remain anonymous
There is no real difference
quiz.e: The key distinction is whether the source's identity is directly attributed.

quiz.q: Which best explains why open questions are favored for feature interviews?
o: They encourage detailed, quotable, reflective responses
They are faster to answer
They require no follow-up
They avoid the need for research
quiz.e: Features often need rich, descriptive quotes that open questions are more likely to produce.

quiz.q: Which best explains why closed questions still have a place in interviews?
o: They efficiently confirm specific facts or details
They should be used for every single question
They eliminate the need for a lead
They are more ethical than open questions
quiz.e: Closed questions are useful for nailing down concrete, verifiable facts quickly.

quiz.q: What should a reporter do if a grieving source declines to answer a question?
o: Respect the decision and move on without pressuring them
Insist they answer since it's needed for the story
Threaten to quote them anyway
End the interview immediately without any further questions
quiz.e: Ethical interviewing respects a source's right to decline, especially amid trauma.

quiz.q: Which of these best reflects proper handling of an evasive answer?
o: Ask a clarifying follow-up rather than accepting the vague response
Publish the vague answer verbatim without context
Assume the source is lying and say so in the story
Move immediately to a completely different topic
quiz.e: Persistent, respectful follow-up is the appropriate professional response.

quiz.q: A source insists on reviewing quotes before publication. What is the standard journalistic practice?
o: Most newsrooms discourage or refuse pre-publication quote approval to preserve editorial independence
Reporters must always comply with this request
This is required by law in the U.S.
It has no bearing on journalistic ethics
quiz.e: Granting quote approval can compromise editorial control and is generally avoided by most reputable outlets.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of asking a source to 'walk me through what happened'?
o: It invites a detailed narrative rather than a short answer
It confirms one specific fact only
It signals the interview is ending
It replaces the need for the Five Ws
quiz.e: This open prompt encourages a fuller, chronological account of events.

quiz.q: If a reporter is unsure whether information was meant to be on or off the record, what should they do?
o: Clarify directly with the source before publishing
Assume it is on the record and publish it
Assume it is off the record and discard it silently
Ask a different source instead
quiz.e: Ambiguity should be resolved directly with the source, not assumed either way.

quiz.q: Why is preparation especially important when interviewing a difficult or evasive source?
o: Well-researched, specific questions are harder to dodge with vague answers
It removes the need for any listening
It guarantees the source will cooperate fully
It replaces the need for follow-up questions
quiz.e: Precise, informed questions leave less room for evasive generalities.

quiz.q: Which statement about note-taking during interviews is most accurate?
o: Detailed notes should be kept even alongside audio recording as a backup
Notes are unnecessary if recording
Only direct quotes should be noted
Notes should be taken after the interview from memory only
quiz.e: Real-time notes protect against recording failures and help capture context recordings miss.

quiz.q: Why do experienced reporters often let a pause linger instead of immediately asking the next question?
o: Sources often fill silence with additional, sometimes more candid, information
Pauses are required by AP Style
It signals disinterest to the source
It ends the interview politely
quiz.e: Strategic silence is a proven technique to elicit more from a source.

quiz.q: A source demands their entire interview be off the record after already speaking on the record. Ethically, the reporter should:
o: Decline, since terms must be set before information is shared
Agree immediately to maintain the relationship
Publish nothing at all from any source going forward
Report the source to their employer
quiz.e: Retroactive off-the-record demands aren't valid; the reporter can ethically use what was already on the record.

quiz.q: Which best describes the purpose of pre-interview research into a subject's public record?
o: To ask sharper questions and identify inconsistencies with prior statements
To write the story without needing an interview
To intimidate the source
To avoid needing a nut graf
quiz.e: Solid research equips the reporter to probe deeper and verify claims.

quiz.q: What is the primary risk of using entirely closed questions throughout an interview?
o: The interview yields only short factual answers with little depth or usable quotes
The interview becomes too long
It violates AP Style
It guarantees leading questions
quiz.e: Relying solely on closed questions limits the richness and quotability of responses.

quiz.q: What are the four core principles of the SPJ Code of Ethics?
o: Seek truth and report it; minimize harm; act independently; be accountable and transparent
Be fast; be first; be loud; be viral
Objectivity; profitability; speed; brevity
Truth; balance; entertainment; loyalty to editors
quiz.e: These four pillars organize the SPJ Code of Ethics' guidance for journalists.

quiz.q: Is the SPJ Code of Ethics legally enforceable?
o: No, it is a set of professional, aspirational guidelines
Yes, violating it can result in criminal charges
Yes, it is enforced by federal courts
It only applies to broadcast journalists by law
quiz.e: The Code is a voluntary professional standard, not law.

quiz.q: What does 'minimize harm' mean in the SPJ Code of Ethics?
o: Treating sources, subjects, and vulnerable people with compassion and care
Never publishing any negative information
Avoiding all stories about crime
Refusing to interview grieving people under any circumstance
quiz.e: Minimizing harm means balancing the public's need to know with compassion for those affected.

quiz.q: Why should journalists verify facts with more than one source when possible?
o: Independent corroboration reduces the risk of reporting an error
A single source is always sufficient for any story
It is required by federal law
It eliminates the need for attribution
quiz.e: Cross-checking with multiple sources strengthens the reliability of reported facts.

quiz.q: Which source type is generally preferred during verification?
o: Primary sources like documents or direct witnesses
Secondary sources like other news reports
Anonymous social media posts
Unverified rumors
quiz.e: Primary sources provide firsthand, more reliable evidence than secondhand accounts.

quiz.q: What should a reporter do with a viral social media claim before reporting it?
o: Independently verify it rather than assuming it's accurate
Publish it immediately since it's already popular
Attribute it to 'the internet' without further checking
Ignore fact-checking since it's already public
quiz.e: Viral claims are especially prone to being false or exaggerated and require verification.

quiz.q: What is a conflict of interest in journalism?
o: A situation where personal ties or biases could compromise, or appear to compromise, objectivity
Any disagreement between two reporters
A factual error in a published story
A dispute between a newsroom and its advertisers
quiz.e: Conflicts of interest involve outside influences that threaten actual or perceived impartiality.

quiz.q: Why should journalists avoid accepting gifts from sources?
o: Gifts can create a real or perceived obligation that compromises objectivity
Gifts are illegal to receive in all cases
It has no ethical significance
Sources are legally barred from giving gifts
quiz.e: Even small gifts can create the appearance of favoritism or influence.

quiz.q: Why does even the 'appearance' of a conflict of interest matter?
o: It can damage public trust in the journalist's objectivity even without actual bias
Appearances are irrelevant to journalism ethics
Only proven bias matters, not perception
It only matters for editors, not reporters
quiz.e: Perceived conflicts can undermine credibility just as much as real ones.

quiz.q: What is plagiarism in a journalistic context?
o: Using someone else's words, ideas, or structure without attribution
Making up quotes that were never said
Publishing a correction
Interviewing multiple sources for one story
quiz.e: Plagiarism is the uncredited use of others' work, distinct from fabricating content.

quiz.q: What is fabrication in journalism?
o: Inventing facts, quotes, sources, or events that did not happen
Copying another writer's sentence without credit
Publishing a delayed correction
Using AP Style incorrectly
quiz.e: Fabrication involves creating false information rather than copying real content.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of fabrication?
o: Inventing a composite source who doesn't actually exist
Quoting a real source accurately
Correcting a misspelled name after publication
Citing a public document
quiz.e: A composite or invented source is fabricated, not real, information.

quiz.q: What is the appropriate consequence for confirmed fabrication at a reputable news outlet?
o: Retraction of the story and accountability measures, often including termination
A quiet, unlabeled edit to the online version
No action if the story was popular
A warning with no further consequence
quiz.e: Fabrication is a severe ethics violation requiring formal retraction and accountability.

quiz.q: How should a minor typo (e.g., misspelled word) typically be handled after publication?
o: It can usually be fixed silently without a formal correction notice
It requires a front-page retraction
It should never be fixed
It requires a lawsuit disclosure
quiz.e: Minor, non-substantive errors are typically corrected without a formal published note.

quiz.q: How should a substantive factual error (e.g., wrong date of an event that changes meaning) be handled?
o: With a clearly labeled, published correction explaining what was wrong
By silently editing the online article with no note
By ignoring it if no one complained
By deleting the entire story
quiz.e: Significant errors require transparency so readers understand what was corrected and why.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a news organization's corrections policy?
o: To maintain transparency and long-term trust with the audience
To punish reporters publicly
To avoid ever admitting mistakes
To satisfy advertisers
quiz.e: Clear correction practices show accountability, which builds credibility over time.

quiz.q: What is an ombudsman (or public editor) at a news organization?
o: An independent reviewer of audience complaints and ethical concerns
A synonym for editor-in-chief
A lawyer who handles libel suits
A reporter assigned to cover the courts
quiz.e: Ombudsmen provide an independent check on the newsroom's practices and ethics.

quiz.q: Why is failing to correct a known error itself considered an ethical failure?
o: It leaves the public misinformed and undermines the outlet's commitment to accuracy
Errors are impossible to identify after publication
Corrections are optional under the SPJ Code
It has no bearing on public trust
quiz.e: Accountability requires actively fixing known mistakes, not ignoring them.

quiz.q: Which best exemplifies 'act independently' under the SPJ Code of Ethics?
o: A reporter declines to cover a story involving a close family member's business
A reporter accepts free tickets from a source
A reporter lets an advertiser dictate story angles
A reporter publishes a friend's unverified claim
quiz.e: Recusing from conflicted coverage preserves independence and impartiality.

quiz.q: Which best exemplifies 'seek truth and report it'?
o: Verifying a claim with original documents before publishing
Publishing a rumor because it seems plausible
Skipping fact-checking to meet a deadline
Reporting only one side of a controversial issue without disclosure
quiz.e: This principle centers on diligent verification and providing full context.

quiz.q: A reporter has a close personal friendship with a political candidate they're assigned to cover. What is the ethical concern?
o: A conflict of interest that could bias or appear to bias the coverage
No concern, since friendships don't affect reporting
A copyright issue
A libel risk only
