A reporting approach that uses data analysis and visualization to uncover and communicate stories.
AI-generated or manipulated video or audio that convincingly depicts events or statements that did not actually occur.
Descriptive information, such as title tags and meta descriptions, that summarizes a webpage's content for search engines.
What a person is actually trying to find or accomplish when entering a search query, which should guide how a story is framed and titled.
A newsroom's formal guidelines on what journalists can post publicly, especially regarding topics they cover professionally.

PART_A.q: Which news value refers to how many people are affected by an event and how seriously?
o: Impact/consequence
Timeliness
Novelty
Proximity
PART_A.e: Impact measures the scale and seriousness of an event's effect on the audience.

PART_A.q: What does 'agenda-setting' theory claim about the press?
o: The media shapes what audiences think about, not necessarily what to think
The media has no influence on public opinion
The media only reports facts with zero selection bias
Agenda-setting only applies to opinion journalism
PART_A.e: Agenda-setting theory holds that prominence in coverage signals importance to the public, even without persuasion.

PART_A.q: What is the primary purpose of the inverted pyramid structure?
o: To present the most newsworthy information first, in case readers stop reading
To build suspense toward a dramatic ending
To organize a story chronologically
To separate fact from opinion
PART_A.e: The inverted pyramid front-loads the most important facts so readers get the key information even if they stop reading early.

PART_A.q: What are the 'Five Ws and H' used for in news writing?
o: Ensuring a story answers who, what, when, where, why, and how
Formatting a headline
Structuring an editorial's argument
Citing legal sources
PART_A.e: The Five Ws and H are the essential questions a complete news story should answer.

PART_A.q: What is the purpose of an open-ended question in an interview?
o: To encourage a detailed, expansive response rather than a yes/no answer
To confirm a fact quickly
To end the interview
To avoid follow-up questions
PART_A.e: Open-ended questions invite subjects to elaborate, producing richer material than closed yes/no questions.

PART_A.q: What does it mean for a source to speak 'on background'?
o: Information can be used but not attributed to the source by name
The interview is entirely off the record
The source must be quoted verbatim
The conversation is recorded for legal purposes only
PART_A.e: On background allows use of the information without directly naming the source, per an agreed arrangement.

PART_A.q: What is the core principle of fact-checking in journalism?
o: Verifying claims against independent, reliable evidence before publication
Trusting any single source without corroboration
Publishing first and correcting errors later as routine practice
Only checking facts that seem controversial
PART_A.e: Fact-checking requires independent verification of claims before a story is published.

PART_A.q: What is plagiarism in a journalism context?
o: Presenting someone else's words or reporting as your own without attribution
Quoting a source with proper attribution
Paraphrasing a press release with credit
Citing a public record
PART_A.e: Plagiarism is using another's work without giving credit, a serious ethical violation in journalism.

PART_A.q: What is the purpose of a nut graf in a feature story?
o: To explain why the story matters after the narrative opening
To conclude the story with a summary
To introduce the reporter
To list the story's sources
PART_A.e: The nut graf tells readers the significance of the story after an anecdotal or narrative lede.

PART_A.q: Which best describes 'show, don't tell' in feature writing?
o: Using concrete sensory detail rather than abstract description
Avoiding all quotes
Writing only in the passive voice
Never describing a physical setting
PART_A.e: Specific, sensory detail creates more vivid and credible scenes than vague, abstract language.

PART_A.q: What distinguishes an editorial from a news article?
o: An editorial represents the publication's institutional opinion, while news reports facts
An editorial is always signed by one reporter
News articles always include the reporter's opinion
There is no meaningful distinction
PART_A.e: Editorials are unsigned, institutional opinion pieces, separate from objective news reporting.

PART_A.q: What is 'false balance' in news coverage?
o: Giving a fringe or unsupported claim equal weight to a well-evidenced position
Reporting only one side of an issue
Never including any opinion content
Balancing a story's word count evenly between sources
PART_A.e: False balance misleads readers by treating a weak claim as equally credible as strong evidence.

PART_A.q: What is the difference between libel and slander?
o: Libel is written defamation; slander is spoken defamation
Libel is spoken; slander is written
They are legally identical terms
Libel applies only to broadcast media
PART_A.e: Libel refers to defamation in written or published form; slander refers to spoken defamation.

PART_A.q: What must a public official prove to win a defamation case?
o: Actual malice — knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth
Simple negligence
Nothing beyond the statement being false
That the reporter disliked them
PART_A.e: New York Times v. Sullivan established the actual malice standard for public officials and figures.

PART_A.q: What is the main goal of SEO in journalism?
o: Structuring content so it is more easily found by search engines and readers
Making headlines as sensational as possible
Removing keywords from articles
Avoiding metadata entirely
PART_A.e: SEO helps accurate journalism reach readers who are actively searching for relevant information.

PART_A.q: Why should content found on social media be verified before republication?
o: Being publicly posted does not make content automatically authentic or accurate
Social media content is always accurate
Verification only applies to print stories
Social posts cannot legally be referenced
PART_A.e: Social media content requires the same verification standard as any other source before being republished.

PART_A.q: What is the difference between hard news and soft news?
o: Hard news covers timely, significant events; soft news covers lifestyle and human-interest topics
Hard news is always shorter than soft news
Soft news requires more fact-checking than hard news
There is no meaningful difference
PART_A.e: Hard news covers urgent, significant events like crime and politics; soft news covers lifestyle and human-interest topics with less time pressure.

PART_A.q: What is a lede in news writing?
o: The opening sentence or paragraph that presents the most important information
The story's headline
The reporter's byline
The final paragraph of a story
PART_A.e: The lede is the crucial opening that conveys the story's most newsworthy information.

PART_A.q: Why is active listening important during an interview?
o: It allows the reporter to ask meaningful follow-up questions based on what the subject actually says
It ensures the reporter never takes notes
It replaces the need for preparation
It guarantees the source will avoid controversial topics
PART_A.e: Active listening lets a reporter follow up on unexpected or important details rather than sticking rigidly to a prepared list.

PART_A.q: What is a conflict of interest in journalism ethics?
o: A situation where a reporter's personal interests could compromise objective reporting
A disagreement between two sources
A type of investigative story
A legal claim against a publication
PART_A.e: Conflicts of interest arise when personal relationships or interests could bias a reporter's coverage.

PART_A.q: What is a 'kicker' in a feature story?
o: The strong closing line, quote, or image that ends the story with resonance
The opening paragraph
The story's headline
A type of fact-check
PART_A.e: The kicker is the memorable final element chosen to leave a lasting impression.

PART_A.q: What is an op-ed?
o: A signed opinion piece by someone outside the publication's staff
An unsigned institutional opinion piece
A straight news story
A press release
PART_A.e: Op-eds are attributed to an outside writer, distinguishing them from unsigned editorials.

PART_A.q: What is the purpose of a shield law?
o: To protect journalists from being legally compelled to reveal confidential sources
To require reporters to reveal all sources
To shield officials from press scrutiny
To block all lawsuits against news organizations
PART_A.e: Shield laws protect source confidentiality so information can flow to reporters without fear of exposure.

PART_A.q: What is a deepfake?
o: AI-generated or manipulated video or audio that convincingly depicts events that did not occur
A verified, authentic photo
A type of SEO metadata
A synonym for a live blog
PART_A.e: Deepfakes present a growing verification challenge because they can convincingly fabricate video or audio.

PART_A.q: What is gatekeeping in journalism?
o: The process by which editors decide which stories reach the public
A legal term for defamation defenses
A type of interview technique
A synonym for fact-checking
PART_A.e: Gatekeeping happens at every editorial stage, determining what stories are covered and published.

PART_A.q: What information typically belongs in the nut graf of a hard news story?
o: Why the story matters and its broader context
The reporter's personal opinion
A detailed physical description of the setting
The story's final conclusion
PART_A.e: In hard news, the nut graf situates the lede within its broader significance and context.

PART_A.q: What is the benefit of preparing research before an interview?
o: It allows the reporter to ask more informed, specific questions
It eliminates the need for follow-up questions
It guarantees the source will not lie
It replaces the need for fact-checking afterward
PART_A.e: Background research helps reporters ask sharper questions and recognize when an answer needs further probing.

PART_A.q: Why do reputable news organizations issue corrections?
o: To maintain accuracy and transparency after publishing an error
To avoid legal liability entirely
Because corrections are optional and rarely used
To replace the need for fact-checking before publication
PART_A.e: Corrections uphold journalistic accountability by transparently fixing published errors.

PART_A.q: What type of feature identifies a pattern occurring across many people or places?
o: A trend story
A profile
A kicker
An editorial
PART_A.e: Trend stories illustrate a broader pattern using multiple examples, distinct from a single-subject profile.

PART_A.q: What is a column, as distinct from an editorial or op-ed?
o: A recurring, signed opinion piece reflecting one writer's consistent viewpoint
An unsigned institutional statement
A one-time guest submission
A straight news report
PART_A.e: Columns run regularly under one writer's byline, unlike unsigned editorials or one-off op-eds.

PART_B1.q: [Application] A local paper covers a minor traffic accident because the driver is a famous actor. Which news value is most responsible for this becoming a story?
o: Prominence
Timeliness
Proximity
Oddity
PART_B1.e: A well-known person's involvement makes an otherwise minor event newsworthy — the definition of prominence.

PART_B1.q: [Application] A hard news story about a factory fire buries the number of injuries in the seventh paragraph. What structural principle has been violated?
o: The inverted pyramid, which requires the most important facts first
The Five Ws and H, which requires alphabetical order
The nut graf rule, which only applies to features
The AP Style rule on numerals
PART_B1.e: Key facts like casualties belong near the top under inverted pyramid structure, not buried deep in the story.

PART_B1.q: [Application] A source suddenly reveals an unexpected, important detail mid-interview that the reporter had not planned to ask about. What should the reporter do?
o: Follow up with clarifying questions based on active listening, even if it departs from the prepared list
Ignore it and continue with the prepared questions only
End the interview immediately
Refuse to include it in the story regardless of relevance
PART_B1.e: Active listening means adapting the interview to pursue newsworthy details as they emerge.

PART_B1.q: [Application] A reporter has one anonymous source for a serious allegation against a public official. What is the best practice before publishing?
o: Seek independent corroboration from additional sources or documents
Publish immediately since one source is always sufficient
Wait for the official to confirm the allegation personally
Rely solely on the source's reputation for honesty
PART_B1.e: Serious claims generally require corroboration beyond a single anonymous source to meet verification standards.

PART_B1.q: [Application] A feature story opens with a vivid scene of a nurse comforting a patient, then in paragraph three explains that the story is really about a nationwide nursing shortage. What is paragraph three functioning as?
o: The nut graf
The kicker
The dateline
The headline
PART_B1.e: The paragraph that reveals why the story matters, after the narrative opening, is the nut graf.

PART_B1.q: [Application] A news article about a new policy uses the word 'controversial regime' instead of 'government.' What issue does this illustrate?
o: Loaded language that may signal bias
A correctly balanced report
A properly labeled editorial
An example of actual malice
PART_B1.e: Word choices like 'regime' carry connotations that can bias a supposedly neutral news report.

PART_B1.q: [Application] A newspaper publishes a leaked but authentic classified document. The government seeks a court order to stop further distribution before it's fully published. What legal doctrine is most relevant?
o: Prior restraint, which courts treat as presumptively unconstitutional
Actual malice, which applies only to defamation
FOIA exemptions, which apply only to record requests
Shield law protections, which apply only to sources
PART_B1.e: Blocking publication in advance is prior restraint, which the Supreme Court has held requires an extremely high burden to justify.

PART_B1.q: [Application] A reporter finds a dramatic photo circulating on social media claiming to show a local disaster. What should they do before using it?
o: Run a reverse image search and verify its date, location, and source
Publish it immediately since it is already public
Assume it is authentic because it has many shares
Credit it to 'social media' without further checking
PART_B1.e: Verification tools like reverse image search are essential before republishing unconfirmed social media content.

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] How do news values and gatekeeping work together to shape what audiences see?
o: Editors apply news values to select stories, and that selection itself sets the public agenda
News values determine legal liability, while gatekeeping determines story length
Gatekeeping eliminates the need for news values
News values apply only to soft news, gatekeeping only to hard news
PART_B1.e: Gatekeepers use news values to choose stories, and those choices shape which topics gain public attention (agenda-setting).

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] Why does the inverted pyramid structure support both readers and editors?
o: It lets readers get key facts quickly and lets editors cut from the bottom without losing essential information
It guarantees a story will never need editing
It replaces the need for headlines
It only benefits editors, not readers
PART_B1.e: Because information is ordered by importance, editors can trim length from the end while preserving the core facts for readers.

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] How does thorough pre-interview research connect to effective fact-checking later?
o: Good research helps reporters ask precise questions and recognize inconsistencies that need later verification
Research replaces the need for any fact-checking
Fact-checking only applies to written documents, not interviews
Research and fact-checking are unrelated processes
PART_B1.e: Preparation sharpens interview questions and helps reporters flag claims that will require independent verification.

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] Why do transparency and corrections matter to maintaining public trust in journalism?
o: Openly acknowledging and fixing errors demonstrates a commitment to accuracy over image
Corrections make a publication appear less credible
Trust depends only on speed of publication
Transparency is only relevant to opinion journalism
PART_B1.e: Visible accountability for mistakes, rather than hiding them, is central to maintaining journalistic credibility.

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] How does descriptive detail support the overall goals of narrative structure in a feature?
o: Specific, sensory detail brings scenes to life, helping the narrative arc engage readers emotionally
Description is unrelated to a feature's structure
Vague description strengthens narrative pacing better than specific detail
Descriptive detail is only used in the kicker

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] Why is the separation between editorial boards and newsrooms important for maintaining objectivity?

It means editorials are illegal
It ensures reporters never have personal opinions

Both are federal laws automatically covering every journalist
Both eliminate the need for factual accuracy
Both apply exclusively to broadcast journalism

SEO always requires sacrificing accuracy for clicks
Ethics and SEO can never be reconciled
SEO applies only to opinion content

o: The most critical Ws (who, what, when, where) are typically answered in the lede, with why and how following
The Five Ws and H apply only to feature writing, not hard news
The inverted pyramid ignores the Five Ws entirely
Why and how must always appear before who and what

o: Both aim to keep personal factors from shaping how facts are reported
Conflicts of interest are unrelated to objectivity
Objectivity requires reporters to have financial stakes in their stories
Avoiding conflicts of interest only matters in opinion writing

Opinions are always facts once published
False balance only concerns editorials, not news

Verification is now less important since technology has improved accuracy

Only using information from official police reports

Wire stories never include the Five Ws

A rare and improper practice not used by real newspapers
